title: The Songbook of Junebug Creek
premise: Cyrus Vane, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter who lives quietly in Junebug Creek, has spent ten years exchanging letters with an anonymous correspondent whose words once pulled her back from the edge of grief. When a new neighbor, Wren Calloway, arrives to restore the old boathouse, Cyrus recognizes his handwriting—and realizes her dearest friend and the stranger next door are the same man, one who knows more about her family's buried past than she ever suspected. As the summer festival approaches, loyalty to the friend who shielded her collides with the truth he's been keeping: that her grandfather's disappearance and his own family are tangled together. At the festival's closing night, Cyrus finally speaks the sentence she has rehearsed for a decade—'I know it was you, and I forgive you'—choosing love and found family over the safe invisibility she built.
about_author: Paloma Whitlock is a former small-town postmistress who spent years reading other people's letters before writing her own stories. She lives on a tidal creek with a deaf old dog and a piano no one plays well.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Hours
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Establishes her ordered life at Junebug Creek: tending the decommissioned lighthouse, writing a stalled novel, and her ritual of rereading ten years of unsigned letters. Emotional beat: comfort shadowed by loneliness; she guards her small safe steps like scripture.

chapters.title: A Truck Full of Salt Air
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. A moving truck rattles into the neighboring boathouse, carrying Wren Calloway—a carpenter with ink-stained fingers and a familiar way of phrasing things. Emotional beat: unease; something about him snags against memory she can't place.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He unpacks a box containing drafts of every letter he ever sent, revealing to readers what Cyrus doesn't know: he wrote them after his brother's boat went down near the lighthouse the night her grandfather vanished. Emotional beat: guilt braided with longing.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Ladder
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. A storm knocks shingles loose; Wren appears with a ladder and stays for lemonade. Their banter feels dangerously easy, like the letters made flesh. Emotional beat: reluctant warmth; Cyrus notices his handwriting on a work order and dismisses the flicker of recognition.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Preparing the lighthouse for the town's centennial festival, she finds her grandfather's old logbook with a page torn out—dated the night of the wreck. Emotional beat: dread; the past begins knocking.

chapters.title: Festival Committee Politics
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The town drags both newcomers into planning the centennial festival; Wren volunteers to rebuild the stage, Cyrus to write the commemorative booklet. Emotional beat: comic friction turning to real partnership over late nights and cold coffee.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Sent
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. She confesses to Wren—without naming him—that she writes to her anonymous correspondent still, though replies stopped two years ago. Wren goes pale; we learn he stopped when his mother's illness consumed him. Emotional beat: intimacy deepening on a foundation of omission.

chapters.title: The Boathouse Floorboards
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Restoring the boathouse, Wren finds his brother's sealed sea bag hidden under the floorboards, containing proof their father sabotaged the Vane boat's radio. Emotional beat: horror; the truth he fled here to escape is literally beneath his feet.

chapters.title: Small Safe Steps
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. A flashback chapter: the grief that broke her at nineteen, the first anonymous letter that arrived 'like a hand out of dark water,' and why she stopped finishing novels. Emotional beat: tender devastation; readers finally see the stakes of the sentence she can't say.

chapters.title: Moths at the Porch Light
chapters.summary: Dual POV. First kiss, interrupted by Wren's phone call from his dying mother. He lies to Cyrus about where he's going. Emotional beat: joy curdling; the reader feels the lie land even as Cyrus smiles.

chapters.title: The Postmistress Knows
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. The elderly postmistress, sorting festival mail, lets slip that the letters were mailed from three towns over—the Calloway family's town—for exactly ten years. Emotional beat: vertigo; suspicion crystallizes.

chapters.title: Handwriting
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. She compares the work order from Chapter 4 to her letters: same slant, same peculiar g. She confronts nothing, but begins testing Wren with details only her correspondent would know. Emotional beat: controlled panic; love and betrayal sharing one body.

chapters.title: What Wren Couldn't Burn
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. His mother dies; among her papers is her confession that she helped cover up the sabotage to protect Wren's father. Wren now holds the truth that would break Cyrus and clear her grandfather's name. Emotional beat: crushing duty; every path costs someone.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. She stands at the lighthouse rail rehearsing the sentence she's carried a decade—not a confession of love, but 'I know it was you.' She practices forgiveness and accusation until they sound identical. Emotional beat: quiet resolve hardening into decision.

chapters.title: Stage Lights and Fault Lines
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Festival week opens; the town celebrates while Cyrus and Wren orbit each other, each holding a detonation. A drunk councilman jokes about the Vane scandal; Wren nearly brawls. Emotional beat: pressure building toward rupture.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Matching the logbook's torn page to ink blots in the sea bag's contents (which Wren, guilt-ridden, left where she might find it), Cyrus learns her grandfather didn't abandon ship—he stayed aboard trying to fix the sabotaged radio. Emotional beat: grief transfigured into fury.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Cyrus demands everything; Wren gives it all—his brother, his father, his mother's cover-up, and the letters. She calls him a coward built from kindness. Emotional beat: the arc's lowest point; both walk away bleeding.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Radio
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Her grandmother reveals she always knew who wrote the letters—she mailed Cyrus's replies herself, believing a broken boy deserved a chance to mend what his family broke. Emotional beat: wisdom reframing betrayal as penance; Cyrus's anger finds somewhere to go.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren packs to leave, leaving the restored boathouse key and his final letter—unmailed, addressed by hand—with the postmistress. Emotional beat: surrender; he chooses her peace over his hope.

chapters.title: Closing Night
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. At the festival finale, the town lights the lighthouse for the first time in decades. Wren is already gone—or so the crowd believes. Cyrus takes the stage to read her commemorative booklet and instead begins reading his last letter aloud. Emotional beat: breathless pivot; the climax ignites.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Dual POV. From the stage, Cyrus says the rehearsed sentence—'I know it was you, and I forgive you'—into a microphone, then runs the length of the creek road to stop Wren's truck at the tide flats. Emotional beat: catharsis; ten years of silence end in one spoken breath.

chapters.title: Junebug Creek, Continued
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Cyrus's POV. One year later: the novel finished, the boathouse a letter-writing workshop for the town's kids, Wren's name carved beside hers on the lighthouse restoration plaque. Final line echoes the first letter. Emotional beat: homecoming; found family, truth chosen, love kept.
